questions.stem: A 20-year-old male presented with cough and breathing difficulty and was diagnosed with emphysema after radiographic examination. Which of the following genetic conditions should be suspected as a possible cause?
questions.stemHtml: A 20-year-old male presented with cough and breathing difficulty and was diagnosed with emphysema after radiographic examination. Which of the following genetic conditions should be suspected as a possible cause?
questions.solution: a-1 antitrypsin deficiency is a genetic condition characterised by low levels or dysfunctional alpha-1 antitrypsin protein. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency: It is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the alpha-1 antitrypsin gene located on Chromosome 14 . The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to panacinar emphysema and the liver, causing cirrhosis due to abnormal protein accumulation. Cystic fibrosis (Option A) is a genetic disorder caused by CFTR gene mutations, leading to thick mucus, chronic lung infections, and bronchiectasis. While it causes obstructive lung disease, emphysema is not typical. Asthma (Option B) is a chronic inflammatory condition causing reversible airway obstruction and episodic wheezing, coughing, and breathlessness. It does not typically result in emphysema or structural lung damage. Bronchiectasis (Option D) is a condition of permanently dilated bronchi due to chronic infections or inflammation. While it causes cough and sputum production, it does not primarily lead to emphysema. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
a-1 antitrypsin deficiency is a genetic condition characterised by low levels or dysfunctional alpha-1 antitrypsin protein.

 

Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency:

  • It is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the alpha-1 antitrypsin gene located on Chromosome 14.
  • The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to panacinar emphysema and the liver, causing cirrhosis due to abnormal protein accumulation.

 

Cystic fibrosis (Option A) is a genetic disorder caused by CFTR gene mutations, leading to thick mucus, chronic lung infections, and bronchiectasis.

  • While it causes obstructive lung disease, emphysema is not typical.

 

Asthma (Option B) is a chronic inflammatory condition causing reversible airway obstruction and episodic wheezing, coughing, and breathlessness.

  • It does not typically result in emphysema or structural lung damage.

 

Bronchiectasis (Option D) is a condition of permanently dilated bronchi due to chronic infections or inflammation.

  • While it causes cough and sputum production, it does not primarily lead to emphysema.

questions.solution: xplanation: Effect Modifier changes the strength or direction of the association between an exposure and an outcome. Here, exercise modifies the association between smoking and lung cancer, making it stronger in those who exercise less and weaker in those who exercise more. Effect modifier: It is a variable that differentially (positively and negatively) modifies the observed effect of a risk factor on disease status. questions.stem: A patient presented with a hard mass over the right tibia, and subsequent imaging revealed the presence of sessile growth in the bone. Biopsy is done later, which shows the presence of “cartilage cap” over the lesion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A patient presented with a hard mass over the right tibia, and subsequent imaging revealed the presence of sessile growth in the bone. Biopsy is done later, which shows the presence of “cartilage cap” over the lesion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: cal presentation is suggestive of osteochondroma, characterised by the presence of cartilage cap over the lesion and sessile growth in the bone, which means the lesion has both bone and cartilage elements together. Osteochondroma (Exostosis): Osteochondroma is one of the most common benign bone tumors , also called exosurface. It looks like a mushroom-like growth coming out of the bone and is in exact continuity with the underlying bone . In osteochondroma, the tumor’s medulla is continuous with the bone medulla (inner part) and its cortex with the bone cortex (outer part), but it is covered by a cartilage cap, which distinguishes it and gives it the name osteochondroma. Histology: It resembles a disorganized growth plate , and they undergo enchondral ossification , with the newly formed bone making up the inner portion of the head and stalk. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 28 y/o G3P2 woman at 39 weeks of gestation has just delivered via vaginal delivery. She has been diagnosed with severe anemia (Hb 8 g/dL). The obstetric team is concerned about the risk of PPH. What is the next best step in her management to prevent PPH?
questions.stemHtml: A 28 y/o G3P2 woman at 39 weeks of gestation has just delivered via vaginal delivery. She has been diagnosed with severe anemia (Hb 8 g/dL). The obstetric team is concerned about the risk of PPH. What is the next best step in her management to prevent PPH?

options.label: D
options.text: Administration of oxytocin infusion for at least one hour after delivery

questions.answerText: Administration of oxytocin infusion for at least one hour after delivery
questions.solution: ta" data-dictid="7e1c459d2b1692777194da47cd13b3">oxytocin infusion for at least one hour after delivery is a crucial step in the active management of the third stage of labor, which can significantly reduce the incidence of PPH . Continuing oxytocin infusion helps maintain uterine contractions and reduces blood loss after delivery. Prevention of PPH Antenatal Measures Intranatal Measures Maintain hemoglobin > 10 g/dL (Option A) Screen high-risk patients and deliver in well-equipped hospitals Conduct blood grouping for all women Localize the placenta in women with previous cesarean delivery using USG/MRI (Option C) Plan delivery of women with morbidly adherent placenta by a senior obstetrician with blood products ready Active management of the third stage of labor Continue oxytocin infusion for at least one hour after delivery in induced/augmented labor Administer oxytocin 5 IU slow IV during cesarean section (Option B) Use Carbetocin (100 μg IV over 1 min.) to prevent PPH Check the uterovaginal canal for trauma after a difficult labor or instrumental delivery Observe for two hours post-delivery to ensure uterus contraction before transferring to the ward Prefer local or epidural anesthesia over general anesthesia in forceps, ventouse, or breech delivery Allow spontaneous placental separation during cesarean section to reduce blood loss Examine the placenta and membranes routinely for completeness @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
ta" data-dictid="7e1c459d2b1692777194da47cd13b3">oxytocin infusion for at least one hour after delivery is a crucial step in the active management of the third stage of labor, which can significantly reduce the incidence of PPH. Continuing oxytocin infusion helps maintain uterine contractions and reduces blood loss after delivery.

Prevention of PPH

Antenatal Measures

Intranatal Measures
  • Maintain hemoglobin > 10 g/dL (Option A)
  • Screen high-risk patients and deliver in well-equipped hospitals
  • Conduct blood grouping for all women
  • Localize the placenta in women with previous cesarean delivery using USG/MRI (Option C)
  • Plan delivery of women with morbidly adherent placenta by a senior obstetrician with blood products ready
  • Active management of the third stage of labor
  • Continue oxytocin infusion for at least one hour after delivery in induced/augmented labor
  • Administer oxytocin 5 IU slow IV during cesarean section (Option B)
  • Use Carbetocin (100 μg IV over 1 min.) to prevent PPH
  • Check the uterovaginal canal for trauma after a difficult labor or instrumental delivery
  • Observe for two hours post-delivery to ensure uterus contraction before transferring to the ward
  • Prefer local or epidural anesthesia over general anesthesia in forceps, ventouse, or breech delivery
  • Allow spontaneous placental separation during cesarean section to reduce blood loss
  • Examine the placenta and membranes routinely for completeness

The child has no significant respiratory symptoms or joint pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: ting with a "slapped cheek" appearance and progressing to a lacy, reticular pattern, is characteristic of the fifth disease, or erythema infectiosum , caused by parvovirus B19. Clinical features of erythema infectiosum Prodromal phase: Low-grade fever, headache, and mild upper respiratory tract infection symptoms. The characteristic rash in this condition is a "slapped cheek appearance”, presenting as erythematous flushing on the face. The erythematous rash spreads to the trunk and proximal extremities as a lacy or reticulated pattern. First disease (Option A) is another name for Measles / Rubeola , an exanthematous illness caused by an RNA virus belonging to the paramyxovirus family. Here, fever occurs before the onset of rash. Second disease (Option B) is scarle t fever , which is characterised by fever and an erythematous rash along with strawberry tongue , caused by Group A βStreptococcus. Sixth disease (Option D) is also known as Roseola infantum or erythema subitum, in which a rash appears once the fever disappears. It is commonly caused by human herpes virus (HHV)-6 and less commonly by HHV-7 and echovirus 16. @Neet_pg_bot

ting with a "slapped cheek" appearance and progressing to a lacy, reticular pattern, is characteristic of the fifth disease, or erythema infectiosum, caused by parvovirus B19.

Clinical features of erythema infectiosum
  • Prodromal phase: Low-grade fever, headache, and mild upper respiratory tract infection symptoms.
  • The characteristic rash in this condition is a "slapped cheek appearance”, presenting as erythematous flushing on the face.
  • The erythematous rash spreads to the trunk and proximal extremities as a lacy or reticulated pattern.


 

 

First disease (Option A) is another name for Measles / Rubeola, an exanthematous illness caused by an RNA virus belonging to the paramyxovirus family. Here, fever occurs before the onset of rash.

Second disease (Option B) is scarlet fever, which is characterised by fever and an erythematous rash along with strawberry tongue, caused by Group A βStreptococcus.

Sixth disease (Option D) is also known as Roseola infantum or erythema subitum, in which a rash appears once the fever disappears. It is commonly caused by human herpes virus (HHV)-6 and less commonly by HHV-7 and echovirus 16.

questions.solution: ta" data-dictid="e42da316b916927771860f0ba81c19">dissection is a surgical emergency without which the patient would die, and does not warrant an obtained consent under emergency circumstances, and so the Surgeon will not be held liable for any unforeseen consequences during/after the procedure under BNS 30 . questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease recently received a compatible donor organ from her brother. The kidney transplant surgery proceeds as planned, but within minutes of reperfusion, the kidney becomes mottled, cyanotic and anuric. What is the cause for this presentation?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease recently received a compatible donor organ from her brother. The kidney transplant surgery proceeds as planned, but within minutes of reperfusion, the kidney becomes mottled, cyanotic and anuric. What is the cause for this presentation?
questions.solution: lass="customMeta" data-dictid="c7c23b05e116927771899b5232b3d7">hyperacute graft rejection due to preformed antibodies in the recipient. Hyperacute Graft Rejection Hyperacute Graft Rejection is the most rapid and catastrophic form of graft rejection, occurring immediately on the operating table or within the first 48 hours of transplantation. Pathogenesis: Hyperacute rejection is caused by preformed circulating IgG antibodies against donor antigens (mainly HLA or ABO), which may arise from prior pregnancies, multiple blood transfusions, or previous organ transplants. Mechanism: Preformed antibodies bind to donor endothelial antigens, activating complement and causing widespread thrombosis, vascular occlusion, ischemia, and graft necrosis, leading to a kidney that rapidly becomes cyanotic, flaccid, and anuric (sometimes with a few drops of blood). Clinical features: Hyperacute rejection presents with a mottled blue ischemic kidney, loss of graft tone, and absent urine output (anuria) or occasionally hematuria (few drops of blood). Immunologically, hyperacute rejection represents a Type II hypersensitivity reaction mediated by antibodies . @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
lass="customMeta" data-dictid="c7c23b05e116927771899b5232b3d7">hyperacute graft rejection due to preformed antibodies in the recipient.

Hyperacute Graft Rejection

  • Hyperacute Graft Rejection is the most rapid and catastrophic form of graft rejection, occurring immediately on the operating table or within the first 48 hours of transplantation.
  • Pathogenesis: Hyperacute rejection is caused by preformed circulating IgG antibodies against donor antigens (mainly HLA or ABO), which may arise from prior pregnancies, multiple blood transfusions, or previous organ transplants.
  • Mechanism: Preformed antibodies bind to donor endothelial antigens, activating complement and causing widespread thrombosis, vascular occlusion, ischemia, and graft necrosis, leading to a kidney that rapidly becomes cyanotic, flaccid, and anuric (sometimes with a few drops of blood).
  • Clinical features: Hyperacute rejection presents with a mottled blue ischemic kidney, loss of graft tone, and absent urine output (anuria) or occasionally hematuria (few drops of blood).
  • Immunologically, hyperacute rejection represents a Type II hypersensitivity reaction mediated by antibodies.

ass="customMeta" data-dictid="d69566338f1692777189ff10521054">histopathology showing intramacrophagic yeast form and (LPCB) mount showing numerous hyaline hyphae with few tuberculate macroconidia (arrows) and many smooth-walled oval microconidia are pointing towards a diagnosis of disseminated histoplasmosis.

Histoplasmosis

Diagnosis

Microscopy:

  • Stained smears of the specimens show small intra- and extracellular yeast cells
 

Culture:

  • Blood agar and Sabouraud agar show characteristic growth
  • White, cottony, mycelial growth with large, thick-walled, spherical spores with tuberculate (finger-like projections)
 

Serodiagnosis:

  • Antibody titers increase in progressive disease
  • Antigen tests on urine and serum are helpful for immunocompromised individuals.

Skin Test:

  • Delayed hypersensitivity to histoplasmin confirms exposure

Treatment

Amphotericin-B (Option B) for two to four weeks, followed by a year of itraconazole (Option A ruled out)

Fluconazole (Option C ruled out): It is usually reserved for less severe infections or maintenance therapy after initial treatment with more potent antifungals like amphotericin-B. 

Surgical resection (Option D ruled out): It may be considered for localised infections or complications like abscesses, but it is not appropriate as a primary treatment strategy for disseminated histoplasmosis.

questions.solution: 09a1501b0a8">thyroid carcinoma Explanation: The clinical scenario suggests P apillary Thyroid Carcinoma , which is common in the 3rd to 4th decade and often follows childhood irradiation. Origin: Follicular cells Genetics: BRAF, RET-PTC Risk factors: Radiation Thyroglossal cyst Hashimoto’s thyroiditis Clinical Manifestations: Seen in the 3rd to 4th decade. Midline swelling in the anterior part of the neck Occasionally, lateral aberrant thyroid is seen. Metastasis: Lymphatic Characteristic histological features include: Papillary projections Optically clear nuclei (Orphan Annie eye nuclei) Pseudo-inclusion bodies Psammoma bodies (Dystrophic calcification). Follicular thyroid carcinoma (Option A): Less associated with radiation exposure and spreads hematogenously; HPE shows follicular cell architecture with capsular and/or vascular invasion, but lacks the nuclear features of papillary carcinoma. Medullary thyroid carcinoma (Option B): Arises from parafollicular C-cells, not follicular cells, and is associated with MEN 2 and elevated calcitonin; HPE shows nests or sheets of polygonal cells with amyloid stroma (Congo red positive). questions.solutionHtml:
09a1501b0a8">thyroid carcinoma

Explanation:

The clinical scenario suggests Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma, which is common in the 3rd to 4th decade and often follows childhood irradiation.

  • Origin: Follicular cells
  • Genetics: BRAF, RET-PTC
  • Risk factors: 
    • Radiation
    • Thyroglossal cyst
    • Hashimoto’s thyroiditis
  • Clinical Manifestations: 
    • Seen in the 3rd to 4th decade.
    • Midline swelling in the anterior part of the neck
    • Occasionally, lateral aberrant thyroid is seen.
    • Metastasis: Lymphatic
  • Characteristic histological features include:
    • Papillary projections
    • Optically clear nuclei (Orphan Annie eye nuclei)
    • Pseudo-inclusion bodies
    • Psammoma bodies (Dystrophic calcification).

Follicular thyroid carcinoma (Option A): Less associated with radiation exposure and spreads hematogenously; HPE shows follicular cell architecture with capsular and/or vascular invasion, but lacks the nuclear features of papillary carcinoma.

Medullary thyroid carcinoma (Option B): Arises from parafollicular C-cells, not follicular cells, and is associated with MEN 2 and elevated calcitonin; HPE shows nests or sheets of polygonal cells with amyloid stroma (Congo red positive).

Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (Option C): Highly aggressive tumor seen in the elderly, not young adults; HPE shows undifferentiated pleomorphic giant cells and spindle cells with high mitotic activity and necrosis, lacking any features of differentiated thyroid cancer.

questions.solution: /strong> Propofol is the IV induction agent of choice in patients with hepatic disease because it has a rapid onset and shorter recovery time, making it safer for these patients. Anesthesia for patients with hepatic diseases: IV induction agent of choice: Propofol Muscle relaxants of choice: Cis-atracurium/Atracurium due to organ-independent Hoffman degradation (do not rely on renal or hepatic clearance) Inhalational agent: Desflurane or Isoflurane, or Sevoflurane Avoid using halothane: Risk of halothane-induced hepatitis Narcotics used: Fentanyl, Sufentanil Sedatives used: Oxazepam, Lorazepam All long-acting narcotics and sedatives should be avoided in Cirrhotic patients. Thiopentone (Option A): Prolonged recovery in liver disease. Etomidate (Option C): Hemodynamically stable but not first choice. Ketamine (Option D): Increases secretions and may worsen encephalopathy. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
/strong>

Propofol is the IV induction agent of choice in patients with hepatic disease because it has a rapid onset and shorter recovery time, making it safer for these patients.

 

Anesthesia for patients with hepatic diseases:

  • IV induction agent of choice: Propofol
  • Muscle relaxants of choice: Cis-atracurium/Atracurium due to organ-independent Hoffman degradation (do not rely on renal or hepatic clearance)
  • Inhalational agent: Desflurane or Isoflurane, or Sevoflurane
  • Avoid using halothane: Risk of halothane-induced hepatitis
  • Narcotics used: Fentanyl, Sufentanil
  • Sedatives used: Oxazepam, Lorazepam
  • All long-acting narcotics and sedatives should be avoided in Cirrhotic patients.

Thiopentone (Option A): Prolonged recovery in liver disease.

Etomidate (Option C): Hemodynamically stable but not first choice.

Ketamine (Option D): Increases secretions and may worsen encephalopathy.

questions.stem: A 35 year old female hiker ascends to 5,000m in 2 days. Within 24 hours, she develops severe headaches, nausea, coordination difficulties, confusion, and occasional hallucinations. On examination, she is ataxic, with a GCS score of 10 and signs of papilledema. What is the next best step in managing this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 35 year old female hiker ascends to 5,000m in 2 days. Within 24 hours, she develops severe headaches, nausea, coordination difficulties, confusion, and occasional hallucinations. On examination, she is ataxic, with a GCS score of 10 and signs of papilledema. What is the next best step in managing this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Immediate descent to a lower altitude and start oxygen therapy.

options.label: B
options.text: Start dexamethasone and monitor for improvement

options.label: C
options.text: Provide hydration, antiemetics, and continue the ascent

options.label: D
options.text: Administer acetazolamide and maintain current altitude for the next 24 hours at least.

questions.answerText: Immediate descent to a lower altitude and start oxygen therapy.
questions.solution: Explanation: The patient’s signs and symptoms are suggestive of a condition known as High-altitude cerebral edema (HACE). Immediate descent to a lower altitude is the most crucial step in the management of HACE to reduce hypoxic stress. Starting dexamethasone can help reduce cerebral edema and inflammation, complementing the descent. Oxygen therapy (Option B) can provide temporary symptomatic relief, but it does not address the need for reducing cerebral hypoxia and edema. While hydration and antiemetics (Option C) can provide symptomatic relief, continuing the ascent is highly dangerous in the context of severe HACE. Acetazolamide is useful for preventing and treating mild to moderate altitude sickness, but it is not sufficient as a standalone treatment for severe HACE. Maintaining the current altitude can worsen the patient’s condition (Option D) . @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

The patient’s signs and symptoms are suggestive of a condition known as High-altitude cerebral edema (HACE).

  • Immediate descent to a lower altitude is the most crucial step in the management of HACE to reduce hypoxic stress.
  • Starting dexamethasone can help reduce cerebral edema and inflammation, complementing the descent.

 

  • Oxygen therapy (Option B) can provide temporary symptomatic relief, but it does not address the need for reducing cerebral hypoxia and edema.
  • While hydration and antiemetics (Option C) can provide symptomatic relief, continuing the ascent is highly dangerous in the context of severe HACE.
  • Acetazolamide is useful for preventing and treating mild to moderate altitude sickness, but it is not sufficient as a standalone treatment for severe HACE.
    • Maintaining the current altitude can worsen the patient’s condition (Option D).

questions.stemHtml: An 80-year-old female patient came with complaints of gradual progressive diminution of vision for 2 years in both her eyes. She reports that over the last year, she noticed an improvement in her ability to read without glasses. options.label: A
options.text: Advise lifestyle modification and review after 3 months.

options.label: B
options.text: Recommend corticosteroids eye drops and reassess in 6 months.

options.label: D
options.text: Prescribe her rigid gas-permeable contact lenses.

questions.solution: gressive loss of vision along with improvement in near vision (referred to as “second sight” ), combined with characteristic slit-lamp findings, is suggestive of Nuclear Cataract, for which phacoemulsification is the treatment of choice. Management: Surgical measures: Mainstay of treatment. Cataract surgeries: ICCE (not preferred now) ECCE SICS (Small Incision Cataract Surgery) Phacoemulsification (most preferred) Followed by IOL implantation: PC-IOL (Posterior chamber-intraocular lens) is preferred. Advise lifestyle modification and review after 3 months (Option A) would not address the cataract directly and would not improve the visual acuity. Recommend corticosteroids eye drops and reassess in 6 months (Option B): The use of topical corticosteroids after cataract surgery reduces postoperative noninfectious inflammation but it is not used as the treatment for nuclear cataract. Prescribe her rigid gas-permeable contact lenses (Option D): Rigid gas-permeable contact lenses are indicated for early-stage keratoconus with astigmatism. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
gressive loss of vision along with improvement in near vision (referred to as “second sight”), combined with characteristic slit-lamp findings, is suggestive of Nuclear Cataract, for which phacoemulsification is the treatment of choice.
  • Management:
    • Surgical measures: Mainstay of treatment.
    • Cataract surgeries:
      • ICCE (not preferred now)
      • ECCE
      • SICS (Small Incision Cataract Surgery)
      • Phacoemulsification (most preferred)
    • Followed by IOL implantation: PC-IOL (Posterior chamber-intraocular lens) is preferred.

 

  • Advise lifestyle modification and review after 3 months (Option A) would not address the cataract directly and would not improve the visual acuity.
  • Recommend corticosteroids eye drops and reassess in 6 months (Option B): The use of topical corticosteroids after cataract surgery reduces postoperative noninfectious inflammation but it is not used as the treatment for nuclear cataract.
  • Prescribe her rigid gas-permeable contact lenses (Option D): Rigid gas-permeable contact lenses are indicated for early-stage keratoconus with astigmatism.

questions.solution: The above features suggest Medulloblastoma, the most common type of primitive neuroectodermal tumour (PNET) and the most common malignant pediatric brain tumour. It predominantly occurs in the first decade of life, with a second peak around age 30. Histology: Characterized by densely packed small round cells with large nuclei and scant cytoplasm. Location: Typically found in the cerebellum (vermis) in children and the lateral cerebellar hemisphere in adults. Clinical Presentation : Symptoms include headache, vomiting, nausea, weakness, papilledema, and ataxia. Diagnosis: MRI is used for imaging. Management: Treatment involves surgical resection followed by radiotherapy and chemotherapy. Association: Medulloblastoma is associated with Turcot's syndrome. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: >The clinical presentation of difficulty seeing objects in the right half of the visual field (nasal from the left field and temporal from the right field ) in both eyes indicates a visual field defect known as Right Homonymous Hemianopia, which occurs due to a defect in the Left Optic Tract ( lesion posterior to the optic chiasma ) affecting fibers from the right visual field of both eyes. 3. Fatal familial insomnia

questions.solution: Correct answer-A) Physostigmine This is a case of Myasthenia Gravis, as diurnal variation of neuro-symptoms is seen, and the ice pack test shows resolution of ptosis. questions.solution: nd tardive dyskinesia can be treated with drugs that inhibit vesicular monoamine transporters (VMAT). As the name suggests, VMATs are transporters of monoamines, especially catecholamines (adrenaline, noradrenaline, and dopamine), within storage vesicles. They are mainly of three types - VMAT 1, VMAT 2 & VAchT. Centrally, this process mainly involves the release of dopamine, which is abnormal in movement disorders involving excessive dopaminergic activity. Definition

Postpartum thyroiditis is an inflammation of the thyroid gland that occurs after childbirth, typically within the first year postpartum

Etiology

  • Autoimmune Factors
  • Genetic Predisposition
  • Hormonal Changes

Clinical manifestations

It has 2 phases which has a clinical progression-

Thyrotoxic phase( 1-4 months) (Option A)

Hypothyroid phase( 4 to 8 months) (Option B)

The hypothyroid phase either leads to euthyroid phase (Option C) or permanent hypothyroidism (Option D).

Investigation

Thyroid Function Tests:

  • TSH: Elevated in the hypothyroid phase, suppressed in the hyperthyroid phase.
  • Free T4: Elevated in the hyperthyroid phase, decreased in the hypothyroid phase.
  • Free T3: May also be elevated in the hyperthyroid phase.

Thyroid Antibodies:

  • Anti-thyroid Peroxidase (Anti-TPO) Antibodies: Often elevated, indicating an autoimmune component.

Treatment:

  1. Hyperthyroid phase- Beta blockers
  2. Hypothyroid phase- Levothyroxine, (25 mcg to 75 mcg)

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with a history of chronic alcohol use presents to the emergency with sudden onset loss of consciousness and seizures. He also shows signs of confusion, apathy, dementia, visual hallucinations and aggressive behavior. An MRI is performed, revealing the findings shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old man with a history of chronic alcohol use presents to the emergency with sudden onset loss of consciousness and seizures. He also shows signs of confusion, apathy, dementia, visual hallucinations and aggressive behavior. An MRI is performed, revealing the findings shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: ith the characteristic MRI findings of high signal intensity in the splenium of the corpus callosum, coupled with the patient's chronic alcohol use, strongly indicates Marchiafava-Bignami Syndrome. Fig: An axial T2-weighted MR image reveals signal abnormalities in the corpus callosum and periventricular white matter. Fig: A sagittal T1-weighted MR image demonstrates corpus callosum atrophy (short arrow). The central layers of the corpus callosum appear hypointense, while the dorsal and ventral layers are spared, creating the characteristic "sandwich sign" (long arrow) Fig: Axial T1 weighted image after fat saturation and gadolinium injection. Peripheral rim enhancement (arrow) of splenium.Diffuse mild cortical and subcortical atrophy is also present. Marchiafava Bignami Syndrome Marchiafava-Bignami Disease : A rare alcohol-related neurological disorder causing demyelination and necrosis of the corpus callosum , due to vitamin B1 deficiency and oxidative stress . Acute : Sudden LOC, seizures, confusion, psychosis. Subacute : Depression, ataxia, apraxia, dysarthria, dyslexia. Chronic : Progressive dementia, hallucinations, delusions, behavioral changes. MRI (Gold standard) : "Sandwich sign" in splenium (T2 hyperintensity, T1 hypointensity, rim enhancement), ± subcortical atrophy. Treatment : IV thiamine, vitamin B complex, folate, amantadine, and strict alcohol cessation. Alcohol Induced Dementia (Option A): Recent memory loss, cognitive decline (incl. language), with ventricular enlargement and cerebral atrophy seen in ~50–70%. Changes may reverse after 1 year of abstinence. Wernicke's Encephalopathy (Option B): Although confusion is present, the classical triad includes ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and confusion. MRI findings would typically show hyperintensities in the periaqueductal gray matter, mammillary bodies, hypothalamus, and medial thalami, which were not observed in this case. Alexander Disease (Option D) is a leukodystrophy that affects the brain's white matter, it typically presents in childhood or early adulthood and is characterized by other clinical features such as developmental delays and seizures, which do not align with this patient's presentation. @Neet_pg_bot

ith the characteristic MRI findings of high signal intensity in the splenium of the corpus callosum, coupled with the patient's chronic alcohol use, strongly indicates Marchiafava-Bignami Syndrome.

Fig: An axial T2-weighted MR image reveals signal abnormalities in the corpus callosum and periventricular white matter.

Fig: A sagittal T1-weighted MR image demonstrates corpus callosum atrophy (short arrow). The central layers of the corpus callosum appear hypointense, while the dorsal and ventral layers are spared, creating the characteristic "sandwich sign" (long arrow)

Fig: Axial T1 weighted image after fat saturation and gadolinium injection. Peripheral rim enhancement (arrow) of splenium.Diffuse mild cortical and subcortical atrophy is also present.


Marchiafava Bignami Syndrome

 

Marchiafava-Bignami Disease:
A rare alcohol-related neurological disorder causing demyelination and necrosis of the corpus callosum, due to vitamin B1 deficiency and oxidative stress.

  • Acute: Sudden LOC, seizures, confusion, psychosis.

  • Subacute: Depression, ataxia, apraxia, dysarthria, dyslexia.

  • Chronic: Progressive dementia, hallucinations, delusions, behavioral changes.

MRI (Gold standard):

  • "Sandwich sign" in splenium (T2 hyperintensity, T1 hypointensity, rim enhancement), ± subcortical atrophy.

Treatment:
IV thiamine, vitamin B complex, folate, amantadine, and strict alcohol cessation.

 

Alcohol Induced Dementia (Option A):Recent memory loss, cognitive decline (incl. language), with ventricular enlargement and cerebral atrophy seen in ~50–70%. Changes may reverse after 1 year of abstinence. 

 

Wernicke's Encephalopathy (Option B): Although confusion is present, the classical triad includes ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and confusion. MRI findings would typically show hyperintensities in the periaqueductal gray matter, mammillary bodies, hypothalamus, and medial thalami, which were not observed in this case.

 

Alexander Disease (Option D) is a leukodystrophy that affects the brain's white matter, it typically presents in childhood or early adulthood and is characterized by other clinical features such as developmental delays and seizures, which do not align with this patient's presentation.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with a slowly enlarging, painless lesion on the neck. She has a history of pulmonary tuberculosis with nodal involvement, treated 3 years ago. On examination, there is a firm, erythematous plaque with crusting and shallow ulceration. Ipsilateral, non-tender cervical lymphadenopathy is also noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old woman presents with a slowly enlarging, painless lesion on the neck. She has a history of pulmonary tuberculosis with nodal involvement, treated 3 years ago. On examination, there is a firm, erythematous plaque with crusting and shallow ulceration. Ipsilateral, non-tender cervical lymphadenopathy is also noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: image suggest a diagnosis of Scrofuloderma, which is caused by the direct extension of an infection (endogenous spread) to the skin from the underlying TB focus (Lymph node, bone joint). It is a multibacillary manifestation and is the most common form of cutaneous TB in children, although it can occur in any age group. It often presents as painless subcutaneous swellings and ruptures into the overlying skin, resulting in discharging sinuses or undermined ulcers or fibrotic scars. The most common focus of infection is the cervical lymph node. The most common sites are the neck and axilla. Biopsy reveals positive staining for acid-fast bacilli and characteristic caseating granulomas seen. Actinomycosis (Option B): Chronic bacterial infection causing indurated nodules or abscesses with sinus tracts and sulfur granules. Unlike scrofuloderma, it lacks caseating nodules. Sporotrichosis (Option C): Fungal infection presenting as painless papules/nodules after trauma, spreading linearly along lymphatics. Unlike scrofuloderma, it lacks central caseation. Pyoderma gangrenosum (Option D) : Rare, non-infectious ulcers with undermined borders, linked to systemic diseases (IBD, RA, hematologic malignancies). Histology shows neutrophilic infiltrate without infection, vasculitis, or granulomas @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: class="customMeta" data-dictid="d9d1e6f2801692777196f37b28fb6a">pneumothorax remains black. So, white lung gives a good contrast to black pneumothorax in expiration. Chest X-ray in Inspiration: Chest X-rays are typically performed during the inspiration phase, which maximizes lung volume and provides a clearer view of the lung fields. During this phase, the lungs fill with air, and the air appears black on the X-ray due to its low density compared to surrounding tissues. {{caption_text}} Chest X-ray in Expiration: Expiratory chest X-rays are utilized for assessing small pneumothoraces and suspected inhaled foreign bodies, while inspiratory chest X-rays are performed in all other cases. {{caption_text}} Appearance During Expiration: When a foreign body obstructs the airway, air may become trapped in the lungs, preventing full exhalation. Consequently, during an expiratory X-ray, the obstructed lung appears black (due to retained air), indicating an obstruction on that particular side. A persistent black appearance in the affected lung can confirm an obstruction. Chest X-ray in Inspiration: Chest X-rays are typically performed during the inspiration phase, which maximizes lung volume and provides a clearer view of the lung fields. During this phase, the lungs fill with air, and the air appears black on the X-ray due to its low density compared to surrounding tissues.

 

 

Chest X-ray in Expiration: Expiratory chest X-rays are utilized for assessing small pneumothoraces and suspected inhaled foreign bodies, while inspiratory chest X-rays are performed in all other cases.

Appearance During Expiration: When a foreign body obstructs the airway, air may become trapped in the lungs, preventing full exhalation. Consequently, during an expiratory X-ray, the obstructed lung appears black (due to retained air), indicating an obstruction on that particular side. A persistent black appearance in the affected lung can confirm an obstruction.

questions.solution: immunocompromised patients (e.g., those with AIDS and low CD4+ counts). questions.stem: Which of the following sequences correctly describes the phases of pathogenesis in Type III hypersensitivity?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following sequences correctly describes the phases of pathogenesis in Type III hypersensitivity?

options.label: A
options.text: Formation of immune complexes → Inflammation and tissue injury → Deposition in blood vessels.

options.label: B
options.text: Deposition of immune complexes → Formation of antibodies → Tissue injury and inflammation.

options.label: C
options.text: Formation of immune complexes → Deposition in tissues → Inflammation and tissue injury.

options.label: D
options.text: Antibody production → Immune complex formation → Activation of cytotoxic T cells.

questions.answerText: Formation of immune complexes → Deposition in tissues → Inflammation and tissue injury.
questions.solution: Phases of Type 3 hypersensitivity: 1. Formation of Immune Complexes : After introducing a protein antigen, antibodies are formed (typically within one week) and react with the antigen in circulation, creating antigen-antibody complexes. 2. Deposition of Immune Complexes : These complexes circulate and are deposited in blood vessels, particularly in organs like the kidneys and joints. Medium-sized complexes formed in slight antigen excess are most pathogenic. 3. Inflammation and Tissue Injury: Deposited immune complexes trigger acute inflammation about 10 days post-antigen exposure, leading to symptoms like fever, joint pain, and proteinuria. Complement activation contributes to tissue injury, with serum C3 levels potentially serving as a marker for disease activity. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Phases of Type 3 hypersensitivity:

1. Formation of Immune Complexes:

  • After introducing a protein antigen, antibodies are formed (typically within one week) and react with the antigen in circulation, creating antigen-antibody complexes.

2. Deposition of Immune Complexes:

  • These complexes circulate and are deposited in blood vessels, particularly in organs like the kidneys and joints.
  • Medium-sized complexes formed in slight antigen excess are most pathogenic.

3. Inflammation and Tissue Injury:

  • Deposited immune complexes trigger acute inflammation about 10 days post-antigen exposure, leading to symptoms like fever, joint pain, and proteinuria.
  • Complement activation contributes to tissue injury, with serum C3 levels potentially serving as a marker for disease activity.

questions.solution: Explanation: In the given scenario, the pregnant woman presents at 37 weeks, the fetal head is not engaged, and the fetal status is stable, which is in a transverse lie. An external cephalic version could be the appropriate next step in management to attempt to reposition the fetus for a potential vaginal delivery. M/c cause of transverse lie - Prematurity It has high risk of cord prolapse Antenatal Management: If there are no contraindications, attempt an external cephalic version (ECV) beyond 35 weeks for the transverse lie. If Version Fails or is Contraindicated: Elective cesarean section (Option D) is the preferred delivery method. Management in Labor : In early labor, try an external cephalic version (ECV) if appropriate or opt for cesarean section if ECV is unsuccessful. In late labor, ECV is usually impractical due to ruptured membranes, so the cesarean section is preferred in such cases. Internal Version Considerations: Only for specific cases like managing the second twin. Immediate induction of labour (Option A): The fetal head is not engaged in the pelvis, which means the baby is not in a favourable position for a safe vaginal delivery. Attempting induction could increase the risk of complications such as cord prolapse or obstruction. Vaginal delivery with careful monitoring (Option C): Vaginal delivery is contraindicated in transverse lie due to the risk of cord prolapse or obstructed labour. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: hronic stable angina, or exertional angina, is a type of ischemic heart disease that occurs when the heart muscle does not receive adequate oxygen due to reduced blood flow through the coronary arteries, especially during physical exertion or emotional stress. Usually lasts 5-10 minutes and resolves with rest or with the use of sublingual nitroglycerin within a few minutes. ECG Findings: Asymptomatic Phase: Normal ECG Symptomatic Phase (During Angina): ST-segment depression (hallmark finding), indicating subendocardial ischemia due to insufficient blood flow to the inner layer of the heart muscle. Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (Option A): While this condition may cause ischemia, it is not typically associated with ST-segment depression on a treadmill test. Prinzmetal Angina (Option B): This type of angina typically occurs at rest, often during nighttime or early morning, and is associated with transient ST-segment elevation rather than depression. Non-ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI) (Option C): While NSTEMI can present with ST-segment depression, the chest pain is more persistent and not typically relieved by rest. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with chronic liver disease is noted to have elevated blood ammonia on laboratory testing. Which of the following is least likely to result from ammonia neurotoxicity?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man with chronic liver disease is noted to have elevated blood ammonia on laboratory testing. Which of the following is least likely to result from ammonia neurotoxicity?
questions.solution: >rigidity Explanation: Elevated ammonia crosses the blood–brain barrier and is detoxified to glutamine in astrocytes. Excess glutamine increases osmotic pressure , leading to astrocyte swelling, cerebral edema, and impaired neurotransmission . Clinical features of ammonia neurotoxicity: CNS dysfunction manifests as tremors, slurred speech, drowsiness, incoordination, visual disturbances , and in severe cases, coma or death . Rigidity involves extrapyramidal/motor pathways , which are not primarily affected by ammonia. Muscle tone is usually preserved in hyperammonemia, helping differentiate it from conditions like Parkinsonism or tetanus. @Neet_pg_bot

Cystinosis

Etiology

Mutations in the CTNS gene (Option C) (encoding the protein cystinosin, a cystine transporter) → Defect in cystinosin → Accumulation of cystine crystals in major organs (kidney, liver, eyes, brain)

Clinical Features

  • Renal: Fanconi syndrome, polyuria, polydipsia, rickets, growth failure

  • Skin/Hair: Fair skin, blond hair

  • Eyes: Photophobia, retinopathy, ↓ visual acuity

  • Other: Fever (↓ sweating), hypothyroidism, hepatosplenomegaly, delayed puberty

Diagnosis

  • Detection of cystine crystals in the cornea.
  • Confirmed by measuring increased cystine content in leukocytes.

Treatment

  • Therapy with cysteamine (converts cystine to cysteine)
  • Cysteamine eye drops for ocular involvement.

questions.solution: ="1" cellspacing="1" style="width:100%"> Medical management of Glaucoma Topical drugs Beta-blockers: Decrease the formation of aqueous humour. Eg: Timolol, betaxolol Alpha agonists: Have dual action i.e. they decrease the formation of aqueous and increase the trabecular outflow. Eg: Adrenaline/epinephrine, dipivefrin, brimonidine, and apraclonidine Miotics: These increase the trabecular outflow and open the angle blockage. Eg: Pilocarpine (Option B ruled out) Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors: These decrease the formation of aqueous. Eg: Dorzolamide and Brinzolamide Newer anti-glaucoma drugs: Netarsudil : Increases the trabecular outflow and also decreases the aqueous production. PGF2 alpha agonist: It increases the uveoscleral outflow For eg- Latanoprost, bimatoprost, travoprost (Option A ruled out) , tafluprost, and unoprostone isopropyl (Option D ruled out) Systemic drugs Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor ​​​​​​​Eg: Acetazolamide Hyperosmotic agents: These draw aqueous out of the eye @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
="1" cellspacing="1" style="width:100%"> Medical management of Glaucoma Topical drugs
  • Beta-blockers: Decrease the formation of aqueous humour.
    • Eg: Timolol, betaxolol
  • Alpha agonists: Have dual action i.e. they decrease the formation of aqueous and increase the trabecular outflow.
    • Eg: Adrenaline/epinephrine, dipivefrin, brimonidine, and apraclonidine
  • Miotics: These increase the trabecular outflow and open the angle blockage.
    • Eg: Pilocarpine (Option B ruled out)
  • Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors: These decrease the formation of aqueous.
    • Eg: Dorzolamide and Brinzolamide
  • Newer anti-glaucoma drugs:
    • Netarsudil: Increases the trabecular outflow and also decreases the aqueous production.
    • PGF2 alpha agonist: It increases the uveoscleral outflow
      • For eg- Latanoprost, bimatoprost, travoprost (Option A ruled out), tafluprost, and unoprostone isopropyl (Option D ruled out)
Systemic drugs
  • Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor
    • ​​​​​​​Eg: Acetazolamide
  • Hyperosmotic agents: These draw aqueous out of the eye

questions.stem: A newborn male presents with severe respiratory distress and a scaphoid abdomen. Chest X-ray reveals bowel loops in the left thoracic cavity. Immediate surgical intervention is planned to repair the diaphragmatic defect. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A newborn male presents with severe respiratory distress and a scaphoid abdomen. Chest X-ray reveals bowel loops in the left thoracic cavity. Immediate surgical intervention is planned to repair the diaphragmatic defect. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: n: Bochdalek hernia is the most common type of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH), accounting for about 90% of cases. The clinical presentation typically includes severe respiratory distress, a scaphoid abdomen, and bowel sounds in the chest, as seen in this patient . A chest X-ray often reveals bowel loops in the thoracic cavity, and immediate surgical repair is necessary. It is usually found on the left side (80%), but can also occur on the right (15%) or be bilateral (5%). Morgagni hernia(Option B) is an anterior, usually right-sided defect, often containing colon, and is usually asymptomatic rather than causing neonatal distress. Rolling hiatus hernia(Option C) occurs in adults when the stomach herniates beside the esophagus, causing reflux or chest pain, not bowel loops in the thorax. Sliding hiatus hernia(Option D) is also an adult condition where the gastroesophageal junction and stomach slide into the chest, presenting with GERD, not neonatal respiratory distress @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
n:
  • Bochdalek hernia is the most common type of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH), accounting for about 90% of cases.
  • The clinical presentation typically includes severe respiratory distress, a scaphoid abdomen, and bowel sounds in the chest, as seen in this patient.
  • A chest X-ray often reveals bowel loops in the thoracic cavity, and immediate surgical repair is necessary. It is usually found on the left side (80%), but can also occur on the right (15%) or be bilateral (5%).

Morgagni hernia(Option B) is an anterior, usually right-sided defect, often containing colon, and is usually asymptomatic rather than causing neonatal distress.

Rolling hiatus hernia(Option C) occurs in adults when the stomach herniates beside the esophagus, causing reflux or chest pain, not bowel loops in the thorax.

Sliding hiatus hernia(Option D) is also an adult condition where the gastroesophageal junction and stomach slide into the chest, presenting with GERD, not neonatal respiratory distress

questions.stemHtml: A 55 y/o male with poorly controlled diabetes presents with a non-healing corneal ulcer in his right eye, despite two weeks of appropriate antibiotic therapy. The ulcer shows signs of impending perforation with severe thinning of the cornea. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Increase the frequency of antibiotic eye drops.

options.label: B
options.text: Apply a pressure bandage and recommend strict bed rest.

options.label: C
options.text: Perform mechanical debridement and apply tissue adhesive glue.

options.label: D
options.text: Start topical steroids to reduce inflammation.

questions.answerText: Perform mechanical debridement and apply tissue adhesive glue.
questions.solution: ong> For impending corneal perforation, necrotic tissue is first removed (mechanical debridement), then tissue adhesive (e.g., cyanoacrylate glue) is applied to seal the thin area and prevent rupture. Mechanical debridement is necessary to remove necrotic material and promote healing in a non-healing ulcer. Tissue adhesive glue is indicated to prevent perforation, especially when the perforation is less than 2mm. Increasing the frequency of antibiotic eye drops (Option A): At this stage, just increasing frequency won’t be useful. Applying a pressure bandage and bed rest (Option B): Pressure can worsen thinning and precipitate perforation. Topical steroids (Option D) are contraindicated as they can worsen the infection. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
ong>

For impending corneal perforation, necrotic tissue is first removed (mechanical debridement), then tissue adhesive (e.g., cyanoacrylate glue) is applied to seal the thin area and prevent rupture.

  • Mechanical debridement is necessary to remove necrotic material and promote healing in a non-healing ulcer.
  • Tissue adhesive glue is indicated to prevent perforation, especially when the perforation is less than 2mm.


Increasing the frequency of antibiotic eye drops (Option A): At this stage, just increasing frequency won’t be useful.

Applying a pressure bandage and bed rest (Option B): Pressure can worsen thinning and precipitate perforation.

Topical steroids (Option D) are contraindicated as they can worsen the infection.

questions.stemHtml: A 23-year-old medical student is studying molecular biology. She learns that a single tRNA molecule can recognize more than one codon for the same amino acid, because base-pairing at the third codon position is less stringent. Which of the following best explains this phenomenon?

options.label: A
options.text: Inosine forming non-standard base pairs at the third codon position.

options.label: B
options.text: The exact matching of all three nucleotides between codon and anticodon.

options.label: C
options.text: Single tRNA binds only to one specific codon.

options.label: D
options.text: The rigid Watson-Crick base pairing at the third position of the codon.

questions.answerText: Inosine forming non-standard base pairs at the third codon position.
questions.solution: ng> Explanation: Wobble phenomenon = flexibility in base-pairing at the 3rd codon position (5’ end of anticodon) . Inosine in the anticodon can pair with U, C, or A , allowing one tRNA to recognize multiple codons. The first two codon bases follow strict Watson-Crick pairing. Clinical relevance: explains the degeneracy of the genetic code and why some mutations at 3rd base are silent. Takeaway: Wobble pairing (via inosine) allows one tRNA to decode multiple codons for the same amino acid. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
ng>

Explanation:

  • Wobble phenomenon = flexibility in base-pairing at the 3rd codon position (5’ end of anticodon).

  • Inosine in the anticodon can pair with U, C, or A, allowing one tRNA to recognize multiple codons.

  • The first two codon bases follow strict Watson-Crick pairing.

  • Clinical relevance: explains the degeneracy of the genetic code and why some mutations at 3rd base are silent.

 

Takeaway:

Wobble pairing (via inosine) allows one tRNA to decode multiple codons for the same amino acid.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male presents with a 3-day history of right lower quadrant pain, fever, and anorexia. His examination is significant for a palpable mass in the right lower quadrant with guarding and rebound. A CT scan demonstrates an appendiceal mass. He was admitted to the hospital and started on intravenous antibiotics. After 48 hours, his fever has resolved, and his abdominal pain has significantly improved. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old male presents with a 3-day history of right lower quadrant pain, fever, and anorexia. His examination is significant for a palpable mass in the right lower quadrant with guarding and rebound. A CT scan demonstrates an appendiceal mass. He was admitted to the hospital and started on intravenous antibiotics. After 48 hours, his fever has resolved, and his abdominal pain has significantly improved. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.solution: this scenario is presenting with an appendix mass . This occurs when the inflamed appendix becomes encased in a phlegmonous mass due to the adherence of the greater omentum and loops of the small bowel. When a patient presents with an appendix mass, the standard treatment is the conservative Ochsner-Sherren regimen , which prioritizes observation and a non-operative approach unless necessary. Given that the patient has demonstrated significant clinical improvement after 48 hours of IV antibiotics, with the resolution of fever and improvement in abdominal pain, the most appropriate next step is to continue the conservative management with IV antibiotics and observe for further improvement. Discharge home on oral antibiotics (Option A): Too early—patient still needs inpatient IV antibiotics and observation until fully stable. Laparoscopic appendectomy (Option C): Not preferred in appendicular mass; high risk of bowel injury due to dense adhesions. Colonoscopy (Option D): Has no role in acute appendicitis; used only in suspected colonic pathology (e.g., carcinoma) @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: a primary hemostasis defect (platelet dysfunction or vWD). Bleeding Time (BT): Prolonged when platelet number or function is reduced → best screening test for primary hemostasis defect. Clotting Time (CT) (Option B) : Measures overall clot formation (intrinsic + extrinsic); normal in isolated platelet defects. Normal CT: 8-15 mins. Prothrombin Time (PT) (Option C): Prolonged only in extrinsic pathway disorders (factor VII deficiency, warfarin therapy). Normal PT: 11-16 secs. Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT) (Option D): Prolonged in intrinsic pathway defects (hemophilia A/B, heparin therapy). Normal aPTT: 25-30 secs. @Neet_pg_bot

  • TVS should be used for a more accurate diagnosis at a β-hCG level of ≥ 1,500 IU/L.

Findings for Diagnosing Unruptured Ectopic Pregnancy

Diagnostic Modality

Findings for Unruptured Ectopic Pregnancy

Transvaginal Sonography (TVS)
  • Absence of Intrauterine Pregnancy: No gestational sac within the uterine cavity when β-hCG ≥ 1500 IU/L.
  • Adnexal Mass: An adnexal mass clearly separate from the ovary (Blob sign) (Option C)
  • Ring-of-Fire Pattern: Increased blood flow around the ectopic mass on Color Doppler (Option D)
  • Presence of pseudo gestational sac.
  • Free fluid in the Pouch of Douglas

Transabdominal Sonography (TAS)
  • Absence of Intrauterine Pregnancy: No gestational sac when β-hCG ≥ 6,000 IU/L
  • Other features: May be visible but less sensitive than TVS for smaller masses

Beta hCG Levels
  • Failure to double the value of β-hCG in 48 hours (Option B)
  • Lower concentration of β-hCG than expected for gestational age

questions.solution: ictid="84294069061692777198bdff94a950">seroma formation Explanation: In this scenario, the accumulation of fluid beneath the graft is indicative of hematoma or seroma formation. This complication can prevent proper adherence of the graft to the wound bed, leading to graft failure if not addressed promptly. Hematomas are collections of blood, while seromas are accumulations of clear fluid. Both can occur when there is inadequate hemostasis or when there is excessive movement or pressure on the graft site post-operatively. Complications of Skin Grafting: Graft Failure (Option A ruled out) : This occurs when the graft does not survive or integrate with the recipient site, due to poor vascularization or improper placement. Infection (Option C ruled out) : Infection typically presents with redness, warmth, and pus rather than just fluid accumulation. Strict sterile techniques during surgery and the use of prophylactic antibiotics can help prevent infections. Hematoma or Seroma Formation (Option B) : Occur when blood or fluid collects under the graft. Proper hemostasis during surgery and the use of drains can prevent this issue. Poor Cosmetic Outcome (Option D ruled out) : If the graft does not match the recipient site's skin texture or thickness, or if it is not placed correctly, the cosmetic result may be unsatisfactory. Complications of Skin Grafting:

  1. Graft Failure (Option A ruled out):
    • This occurs when the graft does not survive or integrate with the recipient site, due to poor vascularization or improper placement.

  2. Infection (Option C ruled out):

    • Strict sterile techniques during surgery and the use of prophylactic antibiotics can help prevent infections.

    • Occur when blood or fluid collects under the graft.
    • Proper hemostasis during surgery and the use of drains can prevent this issue.
  4. Poor Cosmetic Outcome (Option D ruled out): 
    • If the graft does not match the recipient site's skin texture or thickness, or if it is not placed correctly, the cosmetic result may be unsatisfactory.

options.label: A

options.text: U wave begins; ventricular pressure equals aortic pressure; all valves closed

questions.answerText: Second heart sound occurs; ventricular pressure drops rapidly; aortic valve closes
questions.solution: anation : During the isovolumic relaxation phase: It starts with S2 (closure of aortic valve). All valves are closed → no blood enters or leaves. Ventricular pressure falls rapidly as myocardium relaxes. Ventricular volume stays unchanged since valves are shut. T wave (Option A): Ends before isovolumic relaxation. This phase ends when LV pressure falls below LA pressure → mitral valve opens → rapid filling begins. U wave (Option B): Appears after T wave, before P wave. LV pressure < aortic, valves closed, but this isn’t the unique hallmark of the phase. P wave (Option C): Occurs in late diastole (atrial contraction). During isovolumic relaxation, LV volume is constant and tricuspid valve stays closed. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
anation :

During the isovolumic relaxation phase:

  • It starts with S2 (closure of aortic valve).

  • All valves are closed → no blood enters or leaves.

  • Ventricular pressure falls rapidly as myocardium relaxes.

  • Ventricular volume stays unchanged since valves are shut.

 

  • T wave (Option A): Ends before isovolumic relaxation. This phase ends when LV pressure falls below LA pressure → mitral valve opens → rapid filling begins.

  • U wave (Option B): Appears after T wave, before P wave. LV pressure < aortic, valves closed, but this isn’t the unique hallmark of the phase.

  • P wave (Option C): Occurs in late diastole (atrial contraction). During isovolumic relaxation, LV volume is constant and tricuspid valve stays closed.

Osteopetrosis/Marble bone disease: Osteopetrosis is a defect in the osteoclasts . Because the osteoclasts are not functioning properly, bone remodelling and bone resorption are impaired. As a result, the patient ends up with brittle bones , which gives rise to this bone-in-bone appearance . It has multiple inheritance patterns , including autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, and X-linked disorders . Morphologically, affected bones lack internal medullary canal leading to frequent features Osteogenesis imperfecta (Option A): Osteogenesis imperfecta is a collagen defect associated with blue sclera . Rickets (Option C): Rickets is due to vitamin D deficiency. Paget disease of the bone (Option D): It can present with bone pain, deformities, and fractures, but it is very uncommon at a young age and typically occurs in older individuals. It is also considered a pre-malignant condition with an increased risk of osteosarcoma. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 34-year-old male presents with symptoms of acute onset blurred vision, dry mouth, tachycardia, and urinary retention. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his presentation?
questions.stemHtml: A 34-year-old male presents with symptoms of acute onset blurred vision, dry mouth, tachycardia, and urinary retention. His medical history is unremarkable, and he denies any recent illnesses or medication use. On examination, his pupils are dilated and unreactive to light. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his presentation?
questions.solution: opine poisoning (Belladonna poisoning): Atropine is an anticholinergic medication that blocks the action of acetylcholine in the body by binding to muscarinic receptors. In cases of overdose or poisoning, it can cause dry mouth, blurred vision, tachycardia, urinary retention, and dilated pupils, among others. It is treated with physostigmine, which increases ACh levels; it can even cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB) to reverse the CNS effects of atropine poisoning. Cocaine toxicity (Option A): Here the patient is hyperexcitable with tachycardia due to sympathetic discharge. Opioids (Option B): Here, the pupils are not dilated; rather, they are constricted or miotic. Benzodiazepines (Option C): Here, the hallmark feature is respiratory depression . @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
opine poisoning (Belladonna poisoning):
  • Atropine is an anticholinergic medication that blocks the action of acetylcholine in the body by binding to muscarinic receptors.
  • In cases of overdose or poisoning, it can cause dry mouth, blurred vision, tachycardia, urinary retention, and dilated pupils, among others.
  • It is treated with physostigmine, which increases ACh levels; it can even cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB) to reverse the CNS effects of atropine poisoning.

 

Cocaine toxicity (Option A): Here the patient is hyperexcitable with tachycardia due to sympathetic discharge.  

Opioids (Option B): Here, the pupils are not dilated; rather, they are constricted or miotic.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old female presents to the emergency department with altered mental status, flushed skin, and tremors after starting a new antidepressant. On examination, there is hyperreflexia in the lower extremities, muscle rigidity, and clonus. Which syndrome should be considered in her case?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old female presents to the emergency department with altered mental status, flushed skin, and tremors after starting a new antidepressant. On examination, there is hyperreflexia in the lower extremities, muscle rigidity, and clonus. Which syndrome should be considered in her case?
questions.solution: n> Syndrome Explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of Serotonin Syndrome. A potentially life-threatening condition resulting from excessive serotonergic activity. Triggers: Use of serotonergic medications, antidepressants , drug interactions, or overdose (e.g., SSRIs , tramadol). MOA: Increased serotonin synthesis, impaired metabolism, or enhanced receptor activation. Symptoms: Altered mental status (e.g., agitation, confusion) Autonomic instability (e.g., tachycardia, hypertension) Neuromuscular signs (e.g., tremors, clonus) Hyperreflexia, positive Babinski sign, muscle rigidity, and flushed skin. Management: Discontinue serotonergic agents. Supportive care, including IV fluids and benzodiazepines. Malignant Hyperthermia (Option A) occurs in response to certain anesthetic agents, not antidepressants, and presents during or after surgery with muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, and metabolic acidosis. Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (Option C) is triggered by antipsychotics (not antidepressants), it features lead-pipe rigidity and bradyreflexia rather than clonus and hyperreflexia. Heat Exhaustion (Option D) is caused by prolonged heat exposure, it presents with dehydration and fatigue but lacks neuromuscular signs like clonus or hyperreflexia. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
n> Syndrome

Explanation:

The given scenario is suggestive of Serotonin Syndrome.

  • A potentially life-threatening condition resulting from excessive serotonergic activity.
  • Triggers: Use of serotonergic medications, antidepressants, drug interactions, or overdose (e.g., SSRIs, tramadol).
  • MOA: Increased serotonin synthesis, impaired metabolism, or enhanced receptor activation.
  • Symptoms: 
    • Altered mental status (e.g., agitation, confusion)
    • Autonomic instability (e.g., tachycardia, hypertension)
    • Neuromuscular signs (e.g., tremors, clonus)
    • Hyperreflexia, positive Babinski sign, muscle rigidity, and flushed skin.
  • Management: Discontinue serotonergic agents. Supportive care, including IV fluids and benzodiazepines.

 

Malignant Hyperthermia (Option A) occurs in response to certain anesthetic agents, not antidepressants, and presents during or after surgery with muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, and metabolic acidosis.

Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (Option C) is triggered by antipsychotics (not antidepressants), it features lead-pipe rigidity and bradyreflexia rather than clonus and hyperreflexia.

Heat Exhaustion (Option D) is caused by prolonged heat exposure, it presents with dehydration and fatigue but lacks neuromuscular signs like clonus or hyperreflexia.

The researcher collects data from a large sample of adults in the city. Which type of study design is the researcher using in this scenario?
questions.solution: Explanation: A cross-sectional study is used to determine the prevalence of a disease in a population at a specific time. It is also known as a snapshot of the total population. Here it is cross-sectional study because it calculates prevalence of a disease and relies on primary data, i.e., researcher collects the data himself. To assess the incidence, a Cohort study (Option A) starts by determining whether risk factors are present. Case-control study (Option C) determines whether an exposure is associated with an outcome. It starts with diseased and non-diseased. An Ecological study (Option D) compares exposure and disease frequency in a series of populations. The unit of study is population. Ecological study uses secondary data. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: ss="customMeta" data-dictid="f9129e152d16927771960c4ccc40bc">pyruvate dehydrogenase complex is responsible for the irreversible conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, a crucial step in aerobic glucose metabolism. A deficiency in this complex leads to the accumulation of pyruvate, which is then shunted towards lactate production, resulting in lactic acidosis. Clinical Features: Lethargy, vomiting, ataxia , neurological deficits in children Lab: elevated lactate and pyruvate , metabolic acidosis Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex: Increased conversion of pyruvate to ribose-5-phosphate (Option B): Pyruvate does not convert to ribose-5-phosphate (R-5-P), which is produced through the pentose phosphate pathway, and it does not involve the PDH complex. Inhibition of gluconeogenesis in the liver (Option D) would result in hypoglycemia but would not explain the accumulation of lactate and pyruvate. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Where does the data point fall if the Z score equals zero in a normal distribution graph?
questions.stemHtml: Where does the data point fall if the Z score equals zero in a normal distribution graph?
questions.solution: normal distribution curve, the data point falls exactly on the mean if the Z score equals zero. A Z-score shows how many standard deviations a data point is from the mean in a normal distribution. A score of zero means the point is at the mean, positive values indicate it is above, and negative values indicate it is below. The formula for the calculation of the Z score: Z = (x-μ) / σ X - observed value μ - mean σ - standard deviation @Neet_pg_bot

ation:

Rett syndrome:

 

  • X-linked dominant (MECP2 mutation), seen in girls after 6–18 months of normal development.

Cerebral Palsy (Option C): Results in motor impairment and does not involve a period of normal development followed by skill loss.
